reason: council-remediation-2026-07-20/agent-P override of prior batch-062 source-scope retrenchment. The currently linked question states an internal contradiction: it asks for a 'creek easement under PD 1067' but the marked-correct option uses a 4-meter figure that does not exist in Article 51. PD 1067 Article 51 sets easements only by LAND CLASSIFICATION (3m urban / 20m agricultural / 40m forest). No 4-meter rule exists anywhere in the Water Code. This rewrite replaces the fabricated 4m figure with the verified Article 51 land-classification rule.

source_audit_support.source_locator: PD 1067 Article 51. No 4-meter easement appears anywhere in the Water Code. Article body lea-plan-005-05 normalized.md only references PD 1067 easements without specifying 4m.

external_sources.citation: PD 1067 (Water Code of the Philippines), Article 51

proposed.text: A residential lot in an URBAN barangay is bounded along one side by a creek. Under PD 1067 (Water Code of the Philippines), Article 51, what is the public-use easement that must be preserved along the creek bank?

rationale.a: Correct. PD 1067 Article 51 establishes a 3-meter public-use easement along the banks of rivers/streams and shores of seas/lakes in URBAN areas.
rationale.b: Wrong. There is NO 4-meter easement anywhere in PD 1067. The 4-meter figure is fabricated.
rationale.c: Wrong. 20 meters applies in AGRICULTURAL areas, not urban.
rationale.d: Wrong. 40 meters applies in FOREST areas, not urban.
rationale.correct: PD 1067 Article 51: easement of public use is 3 m in urban areas, 20 m in agricultural areas, and 40 m in forest areas. For an urban creek, the correct easement is 3 meters.
rationale.takeaway: PD 1067 easements are determined by LAND CLASSIFICATION (urban/agricultural/forest), NOT by a fixed or per-waterbody-width number. The 4-meter figure seen in some reviewers is not in the statute.

proposed.explanation: For an urban creek, Article 51 fixes the easement at 3 meters. No permanent structures or fences may be built within the easement, which is reserved for public use.
